title: AI scams in Georgia and South Florida: How scammers use deepfakes to steal millions

reading.body:
This is impersonation fraud built on synthetic media. Generative tools were used to clone an immigration attorney's voice and reproduce his identity, and the resulting fake legal service was offered to immigrants over social media and phone calls. The AI is not the system being attacked, it is the instrument that makes a false identity credible enough to be paid. The same reporting describes voice cloning, spoofed numbers and fabricated photographs as general-purpose techniques, with the grandparent scam as the recurring pattern.

The failure sits at the point of contact, where a victim has only a voice, a profile and a phone number to judge. Those are exactly the signals a cloned voice and a spoofed number are built to satisfy, so the ordinary cues people rely on stop discriminating. Catching it would have required verification through a channel the impersonator did not control, such as a number known independently of the call, or a credential checked against its source rather than against the caller's own claim. Banks are reported as saying these attempts are increasingly hard to detect, which places the detection burden on the person being targeted.

What is not established: the reports describe complaints and alleged losses, not adjudicated findings, and no perpetrator has been identified in the material given. The FBI figures are reported losses, not proven ones. The reporting does not state that AI was used in the Cobb County cryptocurrency loss, only that it is described alongside the same scam wave.

summary:
Scammers are increasingly using artificial intelligence to create convincing deepfakes, fake voices, and fraudulent phone calls to steal money from victims. In Georgia and South Florida, criminals have targeted an immigration attorney by cloning his voice and identity, and a Cobb County couple lost approximately $800,000 in a cryptocurrency scam. According to the FBI's 2025 Internet Crime Report, Americans reported nearly $893 million in AI-enabled scam losses last year, with Florida reporting 350 complaints totaling $39.9 million and Georgia reporting 71 complaints totaling $10.4 million. The FBI received over 1 million internet crime complaints overall, resulting in more than $20 billion in losses.

Scammers use generative AI to make traditional frauds more believable by cloning voices from social media, spoofing phone numbers, creating fake photographs, and researching family relationships. The grandparent scam, in which criminals impersonate grandchildren claiming to need emergency money, has become particularly prevalent. Banks warn customers that these impersonation attempts are increasingly difficult to detect. Experts recommend establishing code words with family members to verify identity, verifying urgent requests through known phone numbers, and avoiding immediate money transfers based on phone calls or messages.
